studies.title: By The Quran Of Reminding
studies.meaning: A single letter, then an oath by the Quran described as possessing the reminder. The thing sworn to is not stated, and the classical commentators discuss what has been left out, most of them supplying it from the sentence that follows. Those who reject are in a state of self-importance and division. Then a historical note about generations destroyed who called out when there was no longer any escape, and finally the charge itself: they were astonished that a warner came from among their own, and called him a lying magician.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The opposition described is the leadership of a city that knew the man they were rejecting, which is what the word for astonishment turns on. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The two accusations, magic and lying, were incompatible, since a magician produces real effects and a liar produces none, and the Quran records them together without pausing to point that out.

keyTerms.note: A single letter, recited by name, which gives the surah its title. Most classical commentators decline to interpret the disconnected letters and record the proposals of others without settling among them.
From a root about being hard to reach or overcome. Used of God elsewhere it names unassailability; used of people here it names the posture that comes from thinking oneself so.
A place to slip away to when danger arrives, from a verb about drawing back. The word occurs only once in the whole Quran, in this line about calling out too late.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A warner from among your own people was a specific social problem. A stranger could be dismissed and sent on his way, but a man whose father you knew, whose trades you had witnessed, whose character you had relied on, could not be explained without explaining yourself. That is the difficulty the word for astonishment names, and it is why the response reached for a category rather than an argument.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah opens with one of only three oaths in the Quran sworn by the Quran itself, and another of the three opens the surah standing two chapters before this one. The word used here for the escape that was no longer available occurs nowhere else in the Book, and the classical grammarians wrote at length on the unusual particle that introduces it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The opening establishes that the dispute is not about evidence. The oath names the recitation as possessing the reminder, and then the objection recorded is about the messenger's origins rather than about anything he said. That places the obstacle in the objectors' standing rather than in the content, and the reference to generations who called out too late sets a limit on how long such a posture can be maintained.

crossReferences.why: Opens another surah two chapters earlier with the same kind of oath sworn by the Quran itself.
Records the same astonishment that a man from among themselves was inspired, and the same charge of magic.
States the same reaction in different words, that they wondered a warner had come to them from among them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a piece of advice you dismissed because of who gave it: a sibling, a junior colleague, someone whose life you do not admire. Separate the two questions today. Ask whether the thing was true, on its own, without the person attached to it. That is the whole distinction this opening turns on.

studies.title: Has He Made The Gods One
studies.meaning: The objection is quoted as spoken, and it is about arithmetic. Has he made the gods into one god. That is a very strange thing. Then the leaders walk off and give their people an instruction rather than an argument: keep going, hold to your gods, this is something intended. The last line supplies the reason they offered, that they had not heard of this in the religion of recent times, so it must be an invention. The commentators note that the whole of their answer is about novelty.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical sources connect this passage with a delegation of Meccan notables who went to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) or to his uncle and then left, telling their followers to stand firm. The reports differ in detail and the commentators record them with care. What is not in dispute is the shape of the reply preserved here, which appeals to what was recently customary rather than to any evidence.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the ordinary word for strange. It occurs only once in the Quran, and its exaggeration is part of the quotation, so the surah is preserving their tone as well as their words.
The assembly of notables who spoke for a community. The Quran uses this word repeatedly of the group that opposes a messenger, across many different peoples and periods.
A fabrication put together from nothing, from a root about creating and shaping. The word occurs only once in the Quran, and it names manufacture rather than error.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's leadership did not command; it persuaded and it walked. Notables moved as a group through the city, and being seen to leave a meeting together was itself a public statement that the matter was settled. The instruction they give here, to keep going and hold on, is not policy but morale, and it is the kind of thing said to people who have just heard something they could not answer.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the words in this short passage occur only once each in the whole Quran, the intensified word for astonishing and the word for a thing made up. Both are in the mouths of the opposition rather than in the Quran's own voice, so the surah preserves two pieces of vocabulary it never uses again, apparently because those were the words that were actually said.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The objection concedes more than it means to. Calling the reduction of many gods to one astonishing admits that the claim is intelligible and that its consequences are understood. And the defence offered is about recency, that nobody had heard this lately, which quietly abandons any claim to have reasoned the matter through. The surah lets both admissions stand without comment and moves on to the next question.

crossReferences.why: Records the same appeal to what was found among the fathers as the standing answer of every warned community.
Puts the same complaint to an earlier prophet, asking whether he came to make them leave what their fathers served.
Shows the same leading men speaking to their people about a messenger, and telling them what to think.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you defend a position by saying that nobody does it that way or that it has never been done. Both may be true and neither is a reason. Take one such answer you have given recently and replace it with an honest sentence about why you actually hold the position, even if the honest sentence is that you do not know.

studies.title: Why Him Among Us All
studies.meaning: The last of their objections is the most revealing. Was the reminder sent down on him out of all of us. The complaint is about distribution rather than content, and it names the real difficulty without meaning to. Then the reply comes in two flat sentences, each opening with a particle of correction. Rather, they are in doubt about My reminder. Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment. The commentators read the second as explaining the first: the doubt is comfortable because nothing has cost them anything.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the surrounding ayat record a meeting of the city's leading men. No occasion is reported for this line specifically. In a society where every honour was allocated by rank and negotiated between clans, revelation arriving outside that system was not merely surprising but procedurally wrong, and the objection is phrased exactly as a complaint about an appointment made over the heads of those entitled to it.

keyTerms.note: Literally from between us, an idiom for singling one person out of a group. It concedes that the group had been considered and that the choice fell elsewhere, which is the sting in the objection.
A particle that sets aside what was just said and substitutes something else. It appears twice in this one ayah, so the reply corrects the objection and then corrects its own first correction.
The verb for tasting, used of experience rather than of knowledge. It says the difference between them and belief is not information but something not yet undergone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Precedence in Mecca was tracked with great precision: which clan held the keys to the sanctuary, which provided water for pilgrims, which spoke first at an assembly. Positions were inherited and defended, and a man's standing was known to everyone in the city. A distinction handed to someone outside the expected order upset an arrangement that had taken generations to settle.
studies.didYouKnow: The particle of correction appears twice inside this single short ayah, which is unusual. The Quran uses it to set aside a statement and put another in its place, and here the second use corrects the first, so the objection is answered, and then the answer is deepened, inside one sentence of a dozen words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply refuses to argue about worthiness and redescribes the objection as doubt. That is a claim about what an objection often is: a reason produced afterwards for a position already held. The second correction goes further and locates the comfort of the doubt in the absence of consequence, which is uncomfortable but not vindictive, since the passage stops there and does not describe what tasting it would be like.

crossReferences.why: Records the same objection in fuller form, asking why the Quran was not sent to a great man of the two towns.
Answers the same complaint directly, saying God knows best where to place His message.
Preserves the extreme version, each of them wanting to be handed unrolled scriptures of his own.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you criticised a decision that went to someone else, and check whether your objection was about the decision or about the allocation. Most people can tell the difference if they sit with it for a minute. You do not have to do anything about it. Just name which one it was, honestly, and let that be the whole exercise.

studies.title: Do They Hold The Treasuries
studies.meaning: Two questions and a verdict. Do they have the storehouses of your Lord's mercy, He being the Mighty, the Constant Giver. Or do they hold the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, in which case let them climb up by whatever ropes they can find. The line has an edge of dismissal in it. Then the verdict, in a sentence that is deliberately offhand: an army of the confederates, defeated there. The commentators note the abruptness as itself part of the meaning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The objection just before this was that revelation had gone to the wrong man, which is a complaint about distribution, so the reply asks who is holding the stores. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The last line names the confederates, a word the surah uses again a few lines later for the earlier peoples who combined against their messengers, so the Meccan opposition is placed in that company.

keyTerms.note: The rooms where a household or a ruler kept reserves, and the keys to them were the mark of authority. The question asks who holds the keys rather than who deserves what is inside.
An intensive form from the verb to give freely and without return. It occurs in three ayat of the Quran, and two of the three are in this surah, the second in Solomon's own prayer.

keyTerms.gloss: the ropes, the means of ascent
keyTerms.note: Cords or ties, and by extension whatever a person climbs by. The instruction to go up by them is a challenge with an edge, since the audience had no rope that reached anywhere near.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A merchant's storehouse was the visible measure of his standing, and the keys were carried by the head of the household or given to a trusted man. Disputes about who held keys were disputes about who ran a family. The question here uses that exact picture, and the answer everyone would give is obvious, which is why the passage does not wait for one before moving to the next question.
studies.didYouKnow: The divine name used here for the one who gives freely occurs in only three ayat of the whole Quran, and two of them are in this surah. The second is placed in Solomon's own prayer, so the surah first asks whether the objectors hold the storehouses and then shows a king asking the one who does. The name is not used anywhere else in this chapter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument reduces a complaint about fairness to a question about ownership, and this is the surah's habit. If the objectors do not hold the stores and do not hold the sovereignty, then how a gift is distributed is not a matter they have standing in. The name for constant giving is placed inside the question rather than after it, so generosity is presented as belonging to the one being asked about, not as a concession being requested.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same complaint directly, that God knows best where to place His message and to whom.
Says that if they held the storehouses of mercy they would hold them back for fear of spending them.
Puts the same divine name for constant giving into Solomon's prayer later in this same surah.

studies.applyIt: Notice one place where you are quietly keeping score of what other people have been given: an opportunity, a talent, an easier situation. You do not have to feel differently about it. Just ask the question this passage asks, about who was holding the keys, and then put the ledger down for the rest of the day.

studies.title: A Cry With No Recovery
studies.meaning: Six peoples are listed in two lines and then gathered under one name: those were the confederates. Nothing is narrated about any of them, because the audience knew the stories and the point is the accumulation rather than the detail. One sentence covers all six: not one of them but denied the messengers, so My penalty fell due. Then the present is folded into the same sentence. These are waiting for nothing but a single shout, and the word attached to it means there will be no interval of recovery.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The peoples named ran along the routes the Meccans travelled and through the stories they told, from the flood at the beginning to the dwellers of the thicket in the north. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Calling them the confederates was pointed, since the word describes groups that combine against something, and the surah has just used it of the audience's own leadership a few lines earlier.

keyTerms.note: The pegs driven into the ground to hold a tent. Used as an epithet for Pharaoh in only two ayat of the Quran, and the commentators explain it either as the pyramids or as his manner of punishing.
Groups that band together against something. The surah applies it to six separate peoples across many centuries, which turns them into one alliance running through time.

keyTerms.gloss: an interval, a pause for recovery
keyTerms.note: Originally the time between two milkings of a camel, a short breathing space. The word occurs only once in the Quran, and the denial of it removes any interval at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The gap between two milkings was a real unit of time to people who kept camels, short and familiar, the length of a rest rather than of a journey. Using it as the measure of what will not be granted made the statement precise instead of dramatic. And the peoples listed here were geography as much as history: their ruins and their names were markers on the roads the audience used.
studies.didYouKnow: The name for the dwellers of the thicket appears four times in the Quran with two different spellings, and this surah carries one of the two. The word for the pause that will not be given occurs only once in the Book, and the epithet used here for Pharaoh appears in only one other place, both times without explanation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage compresses many centuries into one sentence in order to make a claim about pattern rather than about any particular people. Denial of messengers is presented as a single recurring act with a single recurring consequence, which removes the possibility that any of these cases was special. Then the present audience is added to the list without a break, which is the whole argument the naming was building toward.

crossReferences.why: Lists several of the same peoples, including the same epithet for Pharaoh, and how each of them ended.
Uses the same word for the confederated parties, each community planning against its own messenger.
Gives a nearly identical list of earlier peoples, ending with the statement that the warning came true.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you keep telling yourself you will get around to when there is a pause. The passage denies exactly that: an interval, a breathing space, the gap between two milkings. There is no pause coming today either. Do the smallest version of the thing inside the crowded day you actually have.

studies.title: Be Patient And Remember David
studies.meaning: They ask for their share to be brought forward before the day of reckoning, which is a taunt dressed as a prayer. The reply is not addressed to them. Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant David, the man of strength, who kept turning back. Then two lines describe what that servant had: mountains glorifying with him at evening and at sunrise, and birds gathered in. The commentators note that the antidote offered for mockery is an account of somebody else entirely.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the demand to bring the punishment forward is recorded in several surahs of this period. No occasion is reported for these ayat. David was known to the Arabs through the scriptural communities they traded with, and this surah introduces him not as a king but as a servant, with the strength and the turning named before the kingdom is mentioned two lines later.

keyTerms.note: A written allotment or a portion assigned to someone. The word occurs only once in the Quran, and using it makes their demand sound like a request for a document rather than for a punishment.
Strength in the sense of capability and firmness, not only physical force. The word occurs twice in the Quran and both are in this surah, the second of a group of earlier prophets.
An intensive form from the verb to come back, so it names a habit rather than a single act. The surah applies it to David here and to his son a few ayat later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Evening and the hour just after sunrise were the two times of day when work paused in that climate: too dark to travel and too hot, respectively. They were also when herds were brought in and when the birds were most visible over a valley. The two moments named here are the ones the audience would have associated with sound carrying across open country.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for David's strength occurs in only two ayat of the Quran, and both of them are in this surah. The word describing him as one who keeps turning back occurs four times in the Book, and three of those four are in this chapter, applied to David, to the birds with him, and to his son Solomon.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction and the example are joined by a conjunction, so patience and remembering are given as one act rather than two. And what is recalled about David is not his victories but his returning, which is the quality a man under pressure would need. The mountains and birds are then introduced as accompaniment to that, so the extraordinary gifts are attached to the ordinary habit rather than the other way round.

crossReferences.why: Records the same gift in different words, mountains and birds echoing with him, and iron made soft.
Says the mountains and the birds were made to glorify along with David, alongside a judgement he gave.
States the wider claim that everything glorifies Him, and that we do not understand their glorifying.

studies.applyIt: The next time somebody says something about you that you cannot answer, do what this ayah does. Do not construct a reply. Read one account of a person who went through worse and kept turning back, and let the reading be your response for that hour. The instruction here pairs patience with remembering somebody else, and the pairing is the method.

studies.title: They Climbed The Sanctuary Wall
studies.meaning: Two gifts are named in a single line: a kingdom made firm, and wisdom together with decisive speech. The second phrase is a technical one, meaning the ability to settle a matter with words, which is exactly the capacity the next scene will test. Then the tone changes into a question addressed to the listener. Has the account of the disputants reached you, when they climbed over into the private chamber. The surah interrupts its own praise to introduce something that came in over a wall.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran gives this account only here, and it gives it in outline. No occasion is reported. The word used for the room David was in is used elsewhere in the Book of the chamber where Zechariah prayed and where Mary was found with provision, so the setting is a place of private devotion rather than a throne room, which is why entry over the wall is described as it is.

keyTerms.note: Literally the cutting of address, an idiom for saying the thing that settles a dispute. The commentators explain it as clarity in judgement and in speech, and the phrase occurs only here in the Quran.
From the word for a wall, so the verb means to come in over one rather than through a door. It occurs only once in the Quran, and it explains the reaction described in the next ayah.
An inner room set apart, used in the Quran of the place where Zechariah prayed and where Mary was found. It is not a throne room, which is what makes the intrusion significant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A ruler in the ancient Near East was reached through a sequence of people: guards, a chamberlain, an appointed hour. Coming over a wall bypassed every one of them, and the shock of it was less about danger than about the collapse of an entire procedure. Anyone who had waited to be heard by a person of authority knew exactly how many stages were being skipped in that one line.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the chamber occurs in four ayat of the Quran, and three of them are about Zechariah and Mary, describing a place of private prayer. The verb for climbing in over the wall occurs only once in the Book, and so does the phrase naming the decisive speech David had just been given, two lines before it is put to the test.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places a gift and a test in consecutive lines without marking the transition. Decisive speech is granted, and then something arrives that will require it under the worst conditions: no preparation, no procedure, and a startled man. That order suggests what such gifts are for. And the setting in a place of private devotion means the interruption comes into the one room a person keeps for himself.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for the chamber, there the place where Zechariah entered and found Mary provided for.
Records another judgement given by David, and says Solomon was made to understand the case.
Describes David being given kingship and wisdom together, after the encounter that made his name.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last interruption that came at the worst moment: a call during dinner, a colleague at your desk as you were leaving. Notice that you probably judged it by its timing before you knew what it was. The next one that arrives today, hear the content first. This passage puts a gift and its test in consecutive lines for a reason.

studies.title: Do Not Fear, Judge Between Us
studies.meaning: They come in on him and he is alarmed. Their first words are reassurance, and then they state their business in a compressed form: two disputants, one of us has wronged the other, so judge between us with the truth. Two conditions follow that are unusual in the mouths of people asking for a ruling. Do not go beyond what is right, and guide us to the level path. The commentators note that they ask not only for a verdict but for direction, which is more than a court is normally asked for.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran narrates this scene only in this surah and gives it without names, dates or setting beyond the chamber. No occasion is reported. Arbitration in the audience's own society worked much as it does here: two parties came to a man of standing, stated their claim, and asked him to decide, and his authority rested on being trusted by both of them rather than on any power to enforce.

keyTerms.note: A sudden alarm at something unexpected, distinct from settled fear. The Quran records the reaction plainly of a prophet, without softening it or explaining it away.
A dual form for two sides of a dispute. It is the ordinary legal word, so the intruders identify themselves by a category anyone would recognise before they say anything else.

keyTerms.gloss: and do not go too far
keyTerms.note: From a root about exceeding a proper limit, used of an unfair or excessive demand. The word occurs only once in the Quran, and it asks the judge to stay inside the case.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dispute in that world went to a man whose judgement both parties would accept in advance, and the asking was formal. You said who you were, you named the other party, and you stated what you wanted decided. Everything in these few words is that procedure, delivered by people who had just come over a wall, which is why the reassurance has to come first.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the disputants use asking the judge not to exceed what is right occurs only once in the whole Quran. Their request ends not with a demand for a verdict but with a request for guidance to the level path, using the same word for a road that the Quran uses of the straight way elsewhere, so a legal petition closes as something closer to a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records fear in a prophet and then has strangers tell him not to be afraid, which is a reversal of the usual direction. It also shows what a request for justice can look like at its best: state the case, ask for truth, ask the judge to stay inside the limits, and ask for direction rather than only for a ruling. That last request is what turns the scene from a hearing into something else.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction that follows this scene, to judge between people with justice and not follow inclination.
States the same standard as a general one, that when you judge between people you judge with justice.
Turns the same request for the level road into the prayer that opens the Quran.

studies.applyIt: The next time you take a complaint to someone, try adding what these two added. Say what you want decided, and then ask the person to tell you if you are the one in the wrong. That second half changes the whole character of the request, and most of us have never once included it.

studies.title: Ninety-Nine And One
studies.meaning: The complaint is given in one sentence and it works entirely by numbers. This brother of mine has ninety-nine ewes and I have one, and he said, put it under my care, and he overpowered me in the argument. Two details do the work. The word for brother, which makes this a claim between people already bound to each other, and the closing phrase, which concedes that the other man won the exchange of words. Nothing is said about force. The wrong described is a wrong done in conversation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Livestock was the ordinary form of wealth across Arabia, and disputes over animals held in common were the commonest kind of case an arbitrator heard. No occasion is reported. The Quran gives this complaint without naming anyone, and the classical commentators discuss the case as it stands rather than as a report about identifiable persons, which is how the surah presents it.

keyTerms.note: A female sheep. The word occurs only in this passage in the whole Quran, and its ordinariness matters, since the case is built from the least remarkable property a person could own.
From the root for taking charge of something on another's behalf. The request is phrased as custody rather than as transfer, which is what makes it hard to refuse.
From a root about being strong and hard to withstand. Applied to an exchange of words it names being beaten in an argument rather than being forced, which is the whole complaint.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Flocks were often run together, with animals from several households grazed and watered as one and the ownership tracked by marks. That arrangement saved labour and generated most of the disputes an arbitrator ever saw. A man with one ewe among a partner's ninety-nine was in a familiar and vulnerable position, and everyone hearing the case would have known someone in it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the ewe at the centre of this case occurs only in this passage in the whole Quran, twice within two ayat and nowhere else. The verb the complainant uses for being overpowered comes from the same root as the word the surah used at its opening for the self-importance of those who reject, so the same strength appears in a boardroom and in a quarrel over one animal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The wrong being described needs no violence and breaks no obvious rule. A request is made politely, pressed hard, and won by force of argument between two parties who were not equals in speech. By putting that case in front of a prophet and a king, the passage says that the small transaction and the large office are governed by the same standard, and that eloquence is a kind of power that can be misused.

crossReferences.why: Gives the judgement on this complaint and then turns immediately to what it revealed to the judge himself.
Names the general standard, that property should not be consumed between you by anything false.
Warns against using an argument before those in authority to take a portion of others' property knowingly.

studies.applyIt: Think of a negotiation you won because you argue better, not because you were right. A refund, a split of chores, a family decision. The complaint in this ayah is exactly that, and nobody involved broke a rule. Go back to one such thing this week and offer the other person the outcome they would have got if they spoke as well as you do.

studies.title: He Realised He Was Tested
studies.meaning: The verdict comes at once and it is confident: he has wronged you by asking for your ewe to add to his own. Then the judge generalises, saying that many partners encroach on one another, except those who believe and do good, and that these are few. And then the sentence turns without warning. David understood that We had been testing him, and he asked forgiveness, and went down bowing, and turned back. The Quran does not say what he understood, and the surah moves straight on.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran gives this scene only here and leaves the nature of the test unstated. The classical commentators divide over it, and many of them explicitly warn against the elaborate stories circulating from earlier scriptural traditions, holding that the text supports only what it says. A common reading among them is that the verdict was given before the second party had been heard, which the scene itself sets up.

keyTerms.note: Partners whose property or interests run together. The word occurs only once in the Quran, and it covers business partners and neighbours whose animals share a pasture alike.

keyTerms.gloss: We put him to the test
keyTerms.note: From the root for smelting metal to bring out what is in it. It names a process of revealing rather than of punishing, which is why the response to it is a request rather than a defence.
To return to something you belong to, used of returning home. The surah has already called him one who keeps turning back, so the verb here is the habit being exercised.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Judgement in that society was given face to face and often quickly, in front of whoever was present. A man of standing who ruled hastily could not quietly revise it later; his word stood in public memory. What the scene records is a private response to a public act, made immediately, and the vocabulary is entirely of return rather than of defence or explanation.
studies.didYouKnow: The printed text carries a mark of prostration at this ayah, one of fifteen such places in the Quran, and reciters prostrate at it. The classical authorities differ over how to classify this particular one, some describing it as a prostration of thanks rather than of recitation, and the sources set out the discussion without treating the difference as a dispute.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Quran leaves the fault unstated, and the classical caution about filling that gap is itself instructive. What the text does record is the sequence: recognition, asking forgiveness, and a physical turning. Nothing is offered by way of explanation to the reader or defence to God. And the general observation about partners is left standing as true, so the verdict is not withdrawn even as the judge's own position is revised.

crossReferences.why: Gives the outcome immediately, that this was forgiven him, along with nearness and a good place of return.
Turns the episode into an instruction about judging between people and not following one's inclination.
States the underlying caution as a general one, verifying a report before acting on what you were told.

studies.applyIt: Recall a judgement you made about someone before hearing their side, and notice that you may still be right. That is not the point of this passage. Go back to that person and ask the question you skipped, without withdrawing anything. What is recorded here is a man who kept his verdict and changed his posture.

studies.title: Nearness And A Good Return
studies.meaning: One short ayah holds the whole outcome. So We forgave him that. The demonstrative is left with no noun attached, so what was forgiven is never named, and the commentators read that gap as deliberate. Then two things are given rather than merely restored: nearness with Us, and a good place of return. Neither is the reversal of a penalty; both are additions. An episode that began with strangers coming over a wall ends with a man closer than he had been before it started.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the close of the episode in the private chamber. No occasion is reported. The Quran gives the forgiveness without stating the fault, and the classical commentators divide over what it was, many of them cautioning against the detailed accounts that entered the commentaries from earlier scriptural traditions. What the surah supplies is the sequence and the outcome, and it moves at once to an instruction about judging.

keyTerms.note: A demonstrative with no noun attached to it. Arabic can point at something already known or deliberately left unnamed, and the commentators read the gap here as intentional rather than as an omission.
A noun for being drawn near, used of approaching a ruler. It occurs in four ayat of the Quran and two of them are in this surah, both of a prophet after a test.
Where a person comes back to at the end, from the verb to return. The word occurs in nine ayat of the Quran, and four of those nine are in this one chapter.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being brought near was a formal matter in the courts of that region. A man was placed closer to the seat of authority, and everyone present could see where he stood, so distance itself was information. The word used here for nearness carries that picture, which means what is described is not a private feeling but a position, granted after an episode that might have been expected to cost one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for a place of return occurs in nine ayat of the Quran and four of them are in this surah, more than in any other chapter. The word for nearness occurs in four ayat, and two of those are here as well. This surah is unusually thick with the vocabulary of coming back and being brought close.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says something specific about forgiveness by what it adds. A pardon that only cancels leaves a person where they were, but here the response to the turning is nearness and a good return, so the episode ends above where it began. That is a claim about the direction of God's dealing with a servant who turns, and it is made without ever naming the offence.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same two words, nearness and a good place of return, for Solomon after his own test.
Shows the same pattern for an earlier prophet, chosen by his Lord after turning, and then guided.
States the general form of the promise, that God forgives all sins for whoever turns back to Him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been forgiven and notice whether you still keep a distance from the person because of it. Most people do. This ayah does not stop at cancelling; it adds nearness. If somebody has forgiven you, close that gap this week with one specific act, and let the forgiveness finish its work.

studies.title: Do Not Follow Your Own Desire
studies.meaning: Authority is given and bounded in the same sentence. The word describing what David is made means one who comes after and stands in another's place, so the office is held on someone else's behalf from the outset. Then two instructions, and the negative one is the more surprising. The danger to a judge is named as his own inclination rather than as bribery or threat. The clause that follows explains the mechanism: desire does not bend the verdict directly, it moves the judge off the path first.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah follows a scene in which two disputants arrive over a matter of sheep and David answers before the second has spoken, then recognises he has been tested and turns in repentance. The classical commentators differ over the details of that account and several treat the reports attached to it with caution, noting that the instruction here is the settled part of the passage.

keyTerms.note: One who comes after another and holds their place. The office is therefore delegated by definition, and the word carries no sense of ownership over what is being administered.
One word covering truth, reality and what is owed. Judging by it means matching the ruling to what is actually the case, not merely following the correct procedure.
From a root meaning to fall or plunge downward. The word hears preference as a slope, which is why the sentence describes it as taking someone off a path rather than as changing their mind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Justice in Arabia was arbitration. A respected man heard both parties in public and his ruling held only because both had agreed in advance to accept him, so his standing for impartiality was the entire basis of the system. Pressure from kin was constant and visible, and an arbitrator who leaned toward his own clan simply stopped being asked. Everybody had watched a hearing and formed a view of the man conducting it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used of David here, for someone placed in the land as a successor, is applied by name to only two figures in the Quran. The other occurrence is in the passage where the angels are told that a deputy is being placed on the earth, before the first human being is made. The word joins a king to the beginning of the human story.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Authority is defined as delegation, which makes it accountable by its nature rather than by a rule added afterwards. The instruction then locates the real threat to fair judgement inside the judge, which is a claim about how corruption actually works: it starts as preference and only later becomes intent. And the closing clause traces the loss of the path back to forgetting a day of reckoning, so justice is tied to memory.

crossReferences.why: Presses the same point further, standing for fairness even where the testimony runs against yourself.
Names the other direction of the same failure, dislike of a people leading to a departure from justice.
Contains the only other use of this word by name, at the placing of a deputy on the earth.

studies.applyIt: Identify one decision coming up this week where one of the options quietly suits you better than the others. Write down which one, before you decide anything, and put the note somewhere you will see it afterwards. The ayah says the tilt happens before the judgement does, which means it can only be caught early.

studies.title: Not Created Without Purpose
studies.meaning: One sentence makes the claim and one names who denies it. We did not create the heaven and the earth and what lies between them as a void thing. The word used covers both purposelessness and falsehood, so the claim is that a world going nowhere would also have a lie built into it. Then the surah does something unusual: it calls the opposite view an assumption held by those who reject, rather than an argument they make, and names what follows from holding it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and it comes immediately after the instruction to David about judging with justice and not following his own inclination. The connection is the point: if the world has a purpose then a judgement inside it matters. No occasion is reported. The Meccan opposition did not deny that God had made the world. What they denied was that it was going anywhere, and this ayah names that as the real dividing line.

keyTerms.note: From a root about a thing being void or coming to nothing. The same word serves for falsehood, so a world without purpose and a world with a lie in it are named by one term.
Opinion held without certainty. Calling their position an assumption rather than a conclusion says it was never argued for, which is a specific charge and a comparatively mild one.
An exclamation of distress rather than a threat with a named agent. Arabic uses it for a state a person falls into, which is why it is attached here to them and to the Fire together.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing in that economy was made without a use. A rope was plaited for a purpose, a well dug for a purpose, a journey undertaken for a purpose, and a man who worked without one was thought to be wasting what he had. Applying the same standard to the sky was not a leap for that audience. It was the question they would have asked about any object of that size.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran makes this same claim in several places, and once it puts the words into the mouths of people at prayer, who look at the heavens and the earth, say that their Lord did not create this without purpose, and then immediately ask to be protected from the Fire. Here the surah reverses that order, stating the fact first and naming the Fire afterwards.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah identifies where the real disagreement lies. Both sides accept that the world was made; they differ over whether it means anything, and the Quran treats that as the point from which everything else follows. It also names the alternative as an assumption, which implies purposelessness is not a finding but a default people arrive at without examining. That is why it is placed beside a judgement given between two men.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same statement in the mouths of people reflecting on creation, who then ask for protection from the Fire.
Asks the human being directly whether he supposed he had been created without any purpose at all.
States that the heaven and the earth and what is between them were not created as an amusement.

studies.applyIt: Take ten minutes today and do something with no use in it at all: sit outside, look at the sky, say nothing. The irony is deliberate. Most people never test whether they believe this ayah, because they never stop long enough to actually look at the thing it is talking about.

studies.title: Shall We Treat Them Alike
studies.meaning: Two questions with the same shape and no answer supplied. Are We to treat those who believe and do good like those who spread ruin in the land. Or are We to treat the wary like the unrestrained. The construction assumes the answer is obvious and does not argue for it. The commentators read this as the surah's reply to the assumption named just before, since a world with no reckoning would be one in which each pair does in fact end up in the same place.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience included people who had watched the honest lose and the ruthless prosper inside their own city, and that observation is what the question addresses. No occasion is reported. Placing it directly after the statement that creation is not purposeless makes the argument run one way: if the outcomes are identical then the assumption would be right, and the surah has just denied it.

keyTerms.note: From a root about a thing going bad, used of rot in food and of the collapse of an order. It names an effect produced in the world rather than a state of the heart.
From a root about placing a shield between yourself and harm. It names attentiveness rather than piety, which is why it can be set against the next word as a matter of conduct.
From a root about splitting something open, used of a person who breaks through restraint in the open. The word occurs in three ayat of the Quran, always against a group described as restrained.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A city that lived by trade depended on people keeping agreements that nobody could enforce. Everyone knew which men could be trusted with a deposit and which could not, and everyone also knew that the second group often did rather better. That gap between conduct and outcome was visible in the market every day, and it is the observation this ayah picks up and answers.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the unrestrained occurs in only three ayat of the whole Quran, and in each of them it stands directly against a group described as dutiful or restrained. The Book never uses it on its own, so the contrast is built into every occurrence, which is exactly how this ayah deploys it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is moral rather than metaphysical and it runs backwards from a conviction most people already hold. If it would be intolerable for the two pairs to end identically, then something must distinguish them, and nothing in this life reliably does. The passage does not prove a reckoning; it shows what denying one would commit a person to. And it leaves both questions unanswered, so the reader supplies it.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question in nearly the same form and calls the judgement they make about it evil.
Puts the shortest version of the question, whether those who submit will be treated like the villains.
Uses the same construction to ask whether those who know and those who do not know are equal.

studies.applyIt: Bring to mind one person who cut corners and did well out of it, and one who did the right thing and paid for it. Hold both in mind for a minute without resolving anything. This ayah offers no relief. It asks whether you actually believe the two of them end in the same place, and it lets you answer.

studies.title: A Book Sent To Be Pondered
studies.meaning: A purpose is attached to the Book, and it is not recitation or assent. It was sent down so that its signs would be turned over and so that people with kernels would take note. The verb means to consider the back of a thing, what trails behind it and follows from it, so what is asked for is working out consequences rather than reading. Then, without a transition, the account of Solomon begins and the next lines are about horses paraded at evening. The reader is handed something to think about immediately.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah opens with the leaders of Mecca walking away from a meeting and telling one another to hold to their gods, and it answers them with a run of prophets who were tested and turned back to God. The instruction to ponder sits in the middle of that sequence, addressed to an audience that had declined to consider the case rather than one that had weighed it and disagreed.

keyTerms.note: From a root suggesting a kneeling camel settling in one place, and so of good that stays and increases. Blessing in Arabic is fixed abundance rather than a wish spoken over something.
Built from the word for the back of a thing. It means following a matter to what comes behind it, so the reflection asked for is about consequences rather than about the surface meaning.
The plural of the inner part of a nut or a seed, the edible core inside the shell. People of understanding are named as people who reach the inside of a matter.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Horses were rare and enormously expensive in Arabia, where camels did most of the travelling and much of the fighting. A stable of trained horses announced both wealth and readiness, and animals were brought out for inspection in the evening once the heat had gone. The word used for their stance describes a specific posture of a well-schooled horse standing at rest.
studies.didYouKnow: One word in these ayat carries a whole description of the stable. It names horses standing on three legs with the edge of the fourth hoof just touching the ground, a posture the classical lexicographers treat as the mark of a trained and well-bred animal at rest. Translations reach for phrases like fine or noble because English has no equivalent term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is given a stated purpose and the purpose is deliberation. The word for those addressed names the kernel inside a shell, which describes understanding as reaching what a matter actually contains rather than what it looks like from outside. Placing that instruction directly before a narrative about a prophet absorbed in his own horses is not accidental. The first thing to be pondered arrives in the next breath.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question as a reproach, whether they ponder the Quran or whether hearts are locked.
Names one specific thing pondering would find, the absence of the discrepancy any other source would leave.
States the other side of the invitation, a book made easy for remembering, repeated four times in that surah.

studies.applyIt: Take one short ayah you already know by heart and spend five minutes not on what it says but on what follows from it. If this is true, what changes about tomorrow. The verb in this passage is about what trails behind a statement, and five minutes on the back of a familiar line is the exercise it names.

studies.title: Until They Were Hidden
studies.meaning: Solomon speaks about horses paraded before him and says something the commentators read in two opposite directions, because the Arabic particle carries both: either he preferred the love of these good things to the remembrance of his Lord, or he loved them on account of that remembrance. Then he asks for them to be brought back and passes his hand over legs and necks, which is read either as care or as their destruction. A third line reports a test, a body placed on his seat, and a turning back.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran gives these three lines and no more, and the classical commentators fill the gaps in very different ways. Many of them explicitly caution against the elaborate accounts that entered the commentaries from earlier scriptural traditions, holding that the text supports only what it states. No occasion is reported. What the surah itself supplies is a review of horses, a recall, a test, and a turning, in that order.

keyTerms.note: To be concealed behind something. The verb occurs only once in the Quran, and the commentators differ over its subject, some reading the sun and others the horses as they went out of sight.
Something that covers or partitions. Read with the sun it means the horizon, and read with the horses it means dust or distance, and the classical sources record both without settling.
To return to where you belong, from the verb used of coming home. The surah applies it to David a few ayat earlier and to Solomon here, in the same form and the same closing position.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Horses were the most expensive thing a ruler could own and the clearest measure of what he could do. They were not transport but capability: speed, reach, the ability to answer a raid before it arrived. Reviewing them was an act of state as much as a pleasure, which is part of why the commentators divide over whether this scene records an indulgence or a duty being carried out.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing something becoming hidden occurs only once in the whole Quran, here, and its subject is not stated, which is why the classical commentators set two readings side by side without choosing between them. The Book gives this episode in three ayat, and every detail later readers wanted, the horses' number, the nature of the body, the content of the test, is absent from all three.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two of these three lines can be read in opposite directions and the tradition preserves both rather than settling them, which is worth noticing in itself. What survives every reading is the last word of the passage: he turned back. The surah has now used that verb of two prophets within ten ayat, in the same form each time, so what is being taught is not what the test was but what was done at the end of it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for turning back, there of David at the close of his own test.
Records another scene from Solomon's life and the prayer he makes after being shown a favour.
States the same danger in general terms, that property and children should not divert from remembrance.

studies.applyIt: Notice the thing you love that is genuinely good: your work, your children, a craft you are proud of. This passage will not tell you whether Solomon was at fault, and the commentators could not agree either. What it does is put a good love and a remembrance in one sentence. Say honestly which of yours came first today.

studies.title: A Kingdom For No One After
studies.meaning: The prayer has two halves and the first is easy to read past. Forgive me, and grant me a kingdom that will not be fitting for anyone after me. The commentators divide over the second request, some reading it as asking for something unique to him and others as asking that nobody after him should need to seek such a thing. He closes on the name for the Constant Giver, which this surah has already used once. What follows is the answer: wind, builders, divers, and others held in fetters.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Solomon was known to the Arabs through the scriptural communities to the north, and stories about his power circulated widely along the routes. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The surah has just described a test and a turning, so the prayer that opens with forgiveness comes immediately after it, and the sequence keeps the request for a kingdom in second place rather than first.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the verb to give freely without return. It appears in three ayat of the Quran and two of them are in this surah, once inside a question and once here inside a prayer.
Moving softly, from a root about slackness and ease. The word occurs only once in the Quran, and it makes the wind under his command mild rather than a storm.
Iron bonds joining a captive's hands to his neck. The word occurs in two ayat of the Quran, and both describe restraint imposed on someone rather than accepted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Building and diving were the two skilled trades that made a coastal economy work: masons who could raise a wall that stayed up, and divers who went down for pearls in the Gulf and came back with what a year of trade depended on. Naming those two occupations turns an account of unseen servants into an inventory of what any ruler in that region would actually have wanted.
studies.didYouKnow: The divine name Solomon uses to close his prayer occurs in only three ayat of the whole Quran, and two of them are in this surah. The first was a question put to the objectors about who holds the storehouses of mercy, and this is the practical answer to it, spoken by a king who asks rather than assumes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of the two requests carries the argument. Forgiveness is asked for first and the kingdom second, and the kingdom is asked for rather than claimed, which places the largest power described in this surah inside a relationship of asking. The gifts are then listed without any comment, and the next ayah calls the whole of it a giving he may distribute or withhold without accounting.

crossReferences.why: Records the same gift of the wind and the same builders and divers working under his command.
Adds detail to the same account, naming what was built for him and how the work was carried out.
Preserves another of his prayers, asking to be enabled to give thanks for what he had been given.

studies.applyIt: Notice the order of your own requests. Most people ask for the outcome first and mention everything else afterwards, if at all. Next time you ask for something specific, put one line before it about what you would want cleared up first. The prayer in this ayah has that order, and the order is doing something.

studies.title: Give Or Withhold, No Account
studies.meaning: The gift is named and then handed over with an unusual freedom: this is Our giving, so confer it or hold it back, without reckoning. The commentators divide over the last phrase, reading it either as no account being taken of how he distributes, or as a giving that has no limit. Then nearness and a good return are named for him, in exactly the words used earlier for David. And the surah turns at once to Job, calling out that hardship and pain have touched him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the move from Solomon to Job is abrupt, from a man with everything to a man who has lost it. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The pairing is this surah's method: two servants receive the same closing formula and the difference in their circumstances is left to speak for itself. What holds the two together is the phrase used of both, Our servant.

keyTerms.note: A noun for a gift rather than a wage, from the verb to hand something over. Naming the kingdom as a gift before granting the freedom to use it removes any question of having deserved it.
To bestow a favour on someone, from the same root as the word for a kindness done without return. It is generosity from a position of advantage, which is what the kingdom had become.
Exertion and the wearing down that comes with it. Another surah uses the same word to say that this kind of toil will never touch the people of the Garden.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A ruler's giving was public and it was remembered. Gifts were made in front of the assembly and recited afterwards by poets, and a reputation for open-handedness could be worth more than revenue. Being told to give or withhold with no account taken describes a freedom no actual ruler in that world had, since every gift and every refusal was counted by somebody who was watching.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming nearness and a good place of return appears twice in this surah, once for David after his test and once here for Solomon after his, in identical words. The word Job uses for the hardship that touched him is the same one another surah uses when it denies that any such toil will reach the people of the Garden.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a maximum of freedom and a maximum of loss side by side with the same closing verdict attached to each. Solomon may give or withhold without accounting, Job has been stripped, and both are called Our servant in the same voice. That says something about where the relationship actually sits: not in the circumstances, which differ absolutely, but in the form of address, which does not.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about nearness and a good place of return, there of David after his test.
Records Job's call in different words, naming the harm and appealing to the Most Merciful of the merciful.
Uses the same word for toil, denying that it or its aftermath will ever touch the people of the Garden.

studies.applyIt: Give something away today without recording it anywhere, including in your own head as a story to tell later. The instruction in this ayah removes the accounting entirely. Most generosity is quietly booked somewhere, and doing one thing outside the ledger is a small experiment in what is being described here.

studies.title: His Family And Their Like
studies.meaning: The restoration is stated in one clause and then doubled: We gave him back his family, and their like along with them. The commentators differ over how to read the doubling, some as the same people returned together with more, others as a further generation. Then two purposes are named for the whole episode and they are unequal in kind. A mercy from Us, and a reminder for those who have kernels of understanding. The suffering and the recovery are both being described as instructive.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah addressed to a small community under sustained pressure. Job was known across the region as the figure who endured, and the Quran gives his account in two places, both of them brief. No occasion is reported for this ayah. What it supplies is the ending, and it says nothing at all about the years in between, which the later tradition fills in various ways.

keyTerms.note: From the same root as the divine name used twice in this surah for the one who gives without return. Using it of a family restored makes people a gift rather than a repayment that was owed.
Something that brings a matter back to mind. It is this surah's own word for itself, so an episode in a man's life is placed in the same category as a passage of revelation.
The plural of the word for the inside of a nut or the pith of a stem. Arabic uses it for the understanding, so those addressed are people who get past the shell of a story.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man in that world without family was without everything: no labour, no defence, no support in old age, no name after him. Losing a household was the completest disaster available, worse than losing property, because property could be rebuilt with your hands and a household could not. Restoration in those terms was not a consolation prize. It was the return of the only security that society had.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran tells Job's story in two places and neither of them describes the affliction itself. This surah gives the call, the instruction about the water, the restoration and the verdict in four short ayat, and another surah gives the whole of it in two. Everything the later tradition supplies about the length and nature of the illness comes from outside the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two reasons are given for what happened, and one of them is not about Job at all. It was a mercy to him, and a reminder to people who would read about it long afterwards, which makes his affliction partly other people's instruction. That is a hard thing to say and the passage says it plainly. The word for those who take the reminder points to understanding rather than to sympathy, so what is asked for is thought.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same restoration in nearly the same words, his family and their like with them, and calls it mercy.
States the same purpose for the accounts of earlier peoples, a lesson for those who possess understanding.
Names what is being tested in such a season and what those who endure it receive in return.

studies.applyIt: Think of a hard season you came out of, and ask who else knows the details of it. Usually nobody, because we tell the summary. This ayah names the account itself as a mercy and a reminder. Tell one person the real version this month, not for sympathy, and let it do the second job the ayah describes.

studies.title: Take A Bundle In Your Hand
studies.meaning: An instruction is given whose background the Quran does not supply: take a bundle of stalks in your hand and strike with it, and do not fail your oath. The commentators explain that an oath had been sworn during the affliction and that this preserved it without harm, and they differ over the details. Then the verdict, which is a summary of a life. We found him patient. What an excellent servant. He kept turning back. The praise names endurance and returning rather than any outcome.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Oaths in Arabia bound a man in a way that is hard to overstate, and failing one damaged his standing permanently, so the difficulty this instruction addresses was entirely familiar to the audience. No occasion is reported. The Quran gives the instruction without the story around it, and the classical commentators supply that background from reports while noting that the text itself states only the resolution.

keyTerms.note: A handful of grass or thin stems gathered together. The word occurs only once in the Quran, and everything the commentators say about this episode turns on what such a bundle is actually like.
From a root about incurring blame, used specifically of not keeping something sworn. The word occurs only here, and it names the thing being avoided rather than the thing being done.
An intensive form from the verb to come back. This surah uses it four times, of David, of the birds gathered with him, of Solomon and of Job, as its highest praise for a servant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath bound a man beyond argument. There was no court to release him and no procedure for revising what had been sworn, so people were extremely careful about what they swore and then lived with it. The difficulty in this ayah, an oath made in extremity that would now cause harm to keep, is one every family in that society could imagine finding themselves inside.
studies.didYouKnow: Both of the unusual words in this ayah occur only once each in the whole Quran: the bundle of stalks, and the verb for failing an oath. The word that closes the ayah, describing him as one who keeps turning back, is used four times in this surah alone, applied to two prophets, to a third, and even to the birds gathered with the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction resolves a genuine conflict without pretending it away. The oath is kept and the harm is not done, which is a specific kind of answer, one that takes both the word and the person seriously. And the praise that follows names patience and returning, two things available to anyone, rather than the healing and the restoration just described. What is commended is what he did, not what happened to him.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same episode in two lines, the call and the restoration, without this instruction at all.
Places the same weight on a confirmed oath, describing it as a bond made with God as guarantor.
Uses the identical words of praise for Solomon, an excellent servant who kept turning back.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise you made that has become hard to keep and that you have been quietly letting lapse. Do not break it and do not pretend it away. Go to the person and say the whole thing out loud, what you promised and why it is now difficult. This passage finds a way to keep the word and avoid the harm, and that conversation is where it starts.

studies.title: Endowed With Strength And Vision
studies.meaning: Six names in two lines, given without any stories. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, described as possessors of hands and eyes, an idiom pairing capability with insight. Then the thing that distinguished them, and it is a single quality: We singled them out with something pure, the remembrance of the Home. Then three more names and a summary, all of them among the best. The commentators note that the quality named is not a deed but an orientation, a habit of keeping the destination in view.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been running through servants who were tested, and it now gathers six more without narrating anything about any of them, which assumes an audience that already knew who they were. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Two of the three named at the end appear in only one other place each in the Quran, so this short list carries a large share of the Book's total mentions of them.

keyTerms.note: Literally possessors of hands, an idiom for capability. Paired with eyes it names the two halves of a competent person, the power to act and the sight to see what should be done.
From the root for a thing being cleared of what was mixed into it. It presents the quality as extracted and set apart rather than as something that simply happened to be present.
A plural of the word for what is chosen and good. It occurs only twice in the whole Quran, and both occurrences are in this passage, one ayah apart from each other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The two words used here, hands and eyes, described how any man was assessed in that world. Could he do the work, and did he see what was coming. Strength without judgement was dangerous and judgement without capacity was useless, and both were said in exactly these terms. Applying the pair to prophets described them in the vocabulary the audience used about their own foremen and guides.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the best ones occurs only twice in the whole Quran and both are here, one ayah apart. Two of the names in the second list appear in only one other place each in the Book, so a passage of five short ayat carries a considerable share of everything the Quran says about those two prophets by name.
studies.theologicalSignificance: One quality is named as the thing that distinguished them, and it is neither an act nor a miracle but the remembrance of the final Home. That moves what makes a life exemplary from what a person does to what they keep in view while doing it. And the list runs across very different circumstances, a migrant, a father, a successor, without distinguishing between them, which is this surah's habit throughout.

crossReferences.why: Names two of the same figures alongside a third, describing all of them as among the steadfast.
Places Elisha inside a longer list of prophets, all of them favoured above the worlds of their time.
States the same purpose for these accounts, that they are a lesson for people who possess understanding.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you kept in view today. Not what you did, which is easier to list. The one quality named in this passage is an orientation rather than an action, a habit of holding the end in mind while doing ordinary things. Set one reminder on your phone for tomorrow that says nothing but the word home, and see what it does.

studies.title: The Gardens With Open Doors
studies.meaning: The description works by removing the small frictions of comfort rather than by piling up luxuries. The doors are not opened when the residents arrive; they stand open already, described with a participle that names a settled state. What is eaten is called for rather than fetched. The companions are matched in age, so nobody is out of place. Then the closing clause names the one anxiety that survives every pleasure and cancels it: this provision has no running out.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah that spends most of its length on prophets who were tested and on opponents who would not listen. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. They arrive at the end of a roll call of earlier prophets, so the garden is presented first as their destination and only then as a promise to the listener. The passage that follows reverses the picture completely for those who transgressed.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle in an intensive form, so the opening is thorough and already done. The gates are not being opened for the arrivals; the state described is how the place stands before anyone reaches it.
The word for leaning on a cushion or an elbow, the posture of someone with no errand to run. In seventh century Arabia it was the position of a host at ease rather than of a servant waiting.
A noun for a supply coming to an end, the way a waterskin or a store of grain does. It occurs in this form once in the Quran, and the denial of it is the last word of the description.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A walled garden in Arabia was an enclosure with a gate, and the gate was kept shut. Water was the reason. Anything green enough to sit under had to be defended from animals, from travellers and from the sun, and the owner controlled who came in. Provision was also seasonal and finite: dates were counted, grain was measured out, and a household knew roughly when the store would run low.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing companions of the same age occurs three times in the Quran, here and in two later surahs. The word for a provision that never runs out occurs only in this ayah. The two details that shape the description, matched age and a supply with no end, are among the rarest vocabulary in the Book's accounts of the Garden.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is described here as a state rather than a set of objects, and the difference matters. Open doors, a reclining posture and an endless supply all name the absence of constraint, which is what the tradition means when it treats the Garden as the removal of every want rather than the satisfaction of a list. The final clause also protects the description from the logic of scarcity that governs every earthly good. Nothing here is being rationed.

crossReferences.why: Describes the gates of the Garden being opened at arrival, where here they are already standing open.
States the same contrast directly: what you hold runs out, and what is with God remains.
Gives the Gardens of Eden again, with angels entering by every gate and greeting the residents.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you hold something back because there might not be enough later: the last biscuit, an hour of your evening, a piece of information a colleague could use. Give that one thing away today without calculating. The ayah closes on a supply that cannot be depleted, and the easiest way to feel the force of that is to act, once, as though scarcity were not the rule.

studies.title: A Crowd Plunging In With You
studies.meaning: A single demonstrative pronoun hinges the surah. It has just closed the description of the Garden, and it opens again here to introduce the opposite, so the two destinies are set side by side by one word used twice. What follows is deliberately unspecific. Two drinks are named, then the text says there are other torments of the same kind without listing them. The scene ends with an arrival announced to those already inside, and the greeting they give is a refusal of welcome.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah whose opening scene has the chiefs of the city walking away from a meeting with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and telling each other to hold to their gods. No occasion is reported for these particular ayat. They belong to the surah's closing argument, where the leaders and the people who followed them are shown together, after the end, saying what they think of one another.

keyTerms.note: The word for a spread bedding or the flat place a child is laid down in. Used of the Fire it is bitterly ironic, since the same root elsewhere describes the earth made level and comfortable for people.

A word the commentators explain variously as intense cold, as what oozes from wounds, and as something foul smelling. They record the range rather than settling it. It occurs twice in the Quran, here and in one later surah.

An eighth form participle from a root for forcing your way into something difficult or dangerous. The same root names the steep ascent nobody attempts in a short Meccan surah, so the word implies effort, not drifting.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab hospitality ran on a formula. A traveller reaching a camp was met with words of welcome, then water, then food, before anyone asked his business, and to withhold the greeting was a public act with consequences. Tribes could be shamed for it for generations. The exchange in these ayat takes that formula and inverts it at the moment of arrival, which is why the refusal of welcome lands harder than the descriptions of heat around it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the cold drink here occurs twice in the Quran, and both places pair it with boiling water, so the two extremes always arrive together. Classical reciters also record a difference over whether the word carries a doubled letter, which changes it from a noun for what flows to an intensive description. The two readings are transmitted side by side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to make suffering picturesque. It names two things and then declines to continue, saying only that there are others of the same kind, which leaves the description short of anything the imagination can settle into. What it does develop at length is the social collapse: the first thing shown inside is people turning on one another. The Quran treats that, rather than the heat, as the substance of the loss.

crossReferences.why: Names the same two drinks together as the recompense, in the Quran's only other use of the word.
Shows the same argument between the weak and those they followed, with the leaders admitting they can offer nothing.
Uses the same verb for plunging into difficulty, there of a steep road of generosity nobody takes.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group you belong to mainly because leaving would be awkward: a chat thread, a circle at work, a habit shared with friends. Ask yourself one question about it today. If this went badly, would these people stand by me, or would we blame each other. You do not have to act on the answer. Just get it clear.

studies.title: No Welcome Either Way
studies.meaning: The reply is an exact return of the words just spoken. Leaders greet the arriving followers by denying them welcome, and the followers hand the same phrase straight back. Then comes the accusation, and it is about sequence rather than force: you are the ones who sent this on ahead for us. The verb is the ordinary one for forwarding goods or dispatching something in advance, so the charge is that the leaders arranged the outcome long before anyone arrived to meet it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the last section of a surah that has spent its length on opposition to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the city. No occasion is reported for the single ayah. Its setting is the surah's closing scene rather than an event: a dispute among the people of the Fire, which the next ayat call true and then use as the reason the warner keeps warning.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning wide or spacious. The Arabic greeting literally offers a broad place to the guest, so denying it is denying room. The word appears in the Quran only in this exchange, twice, once from each side.
