A verb for putting something forward in time or place, used of goods forwarded to a destination and of deeds sent on before a person arrives. The accusation borrows the Quran's own vocabulary for what awaits you.
A noun for where something settles and stays, from the verb for coming to rest. The bitterness is in the permanence rather than the pain: what is called miserable here is the fact of staying.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on patronage. A man without a powerful protector could not trade safely, travel, or expect redress if he was wronged, so ordinary people attached themselves to a chief and took his positions as their own. The arrangement was rarely written down and never equal. What these ayat picture is that structure at the moment it stops paying: the follower discovers he has no standing, and the patron has nothing left to give.
studies.didYouKnow: The greeting denied here appears in the Quran only in these two ayat, and it is the same word Arabic speakers still use to say welcome today. A Book that reports long speeches from prophets and kings gives this everyday courtesy exactly two outings, both of them negative, and both inside one argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is distributed here without being divided. The followers blame the leaders and the blame is not corrected, yet nobody is released by it either, and the next ayat show them asking for the leaders to be punished more rather than for themselves to be spared. The Quran lets both things stand: influence is real and carries weight, and being influenced was still something each person did.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same argument at length, the followers and the followed trading blame until both conceal regret.
Has each group curse the one that entered before it, and both are told they have double.
Shows the bonds between them cut, and the followers wishing for a return they will not get.

studies.applyIt: Pick one opinion you hold strongly and try to name where you first got it. Not the argument for it, the source. If the honest answer is a person or a group rather than something you worked out, that is worth knowing before it matters. You can keep the opinion. Just hold it as yours now, and be able to say why.

studies.title: The Men We Counted Wicked
studies.meaning: A request, then a search, and both are revealing. First the followers ask not for relief but for their misleaders to be punished twice over, which is a prayer with no benefit to the person praying. Then they look around for people they expected to find there. The men they mocked in the world are missing, and they consider two explanations: either the mockery was misplaced, or their eyes have slipped past them. The commentators note that neither option occurs to them until now.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah belongs to the period when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was gathering a following largely from the city's poorer households and its dependents, and when the men of standing found the company he kept a reason to dismiss him. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat, but the classical commentators read the missing men as the believers who had been named and laughed at by name.

keyTerms.note: A noun for a thing doubled or a fold laid over itself. The request asks for the same portion again rather than a different penalty, so even in accusation the vocabulary stays quantitative.
A plural of the word for bad, used as a social label rather than a moral verdict. It occurs once in the Quran, in this ayah, and it is spoken by people describing the believers they looked down on.

A verb for something going off true, used of eyes at the moment they lose a target and elsewhere of hearts turning aside. Choosing it here makes the second possibility a failure of vision rather than of memory.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was small enough that everyone knew who everyone was. Status was read from a man's clothing, his escort, the seat he took at an assembly and whether people rose when he entered. The early believers included freed slaves, foreigners and young men from minor branches of the tribes, and the surviving accounts of Meccan ridicule are consistently about rank rather than argument. These ayat put those two groups in a room after the fact and let one look for the other.
studies.didYouKnow: The word written for mockery here occurs three times in the Quran. In two places it clearly means ridicule. In the third, about people made useful to one another, the classical readers take it as subjection instead, and the whole difference is carried by one short vowel that the earliest copies did not write. The plural used for the wicked occurs only here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mockery is treated as a judgement, not a joke. To laugh at someone is to place them, and these ayat show the placement being checked against the outcome. What makes the scene severe is not that the mockers were wrong about the future but that they had built a whole social world on a ranking they never examined. The Quran returns to this repeatedly, and always by showing the ranking reversed rather than by arguing against it.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same reversal in full, the mockers watched at the end by the people they laughed at.
Instructs the Prophet to stay with those whose company the powerful found beneath them.
Shows the same group told they made others a laughing stock, and forgot the remembrance.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person you find slightly ridiculous. Not someone who has harmed you, just someone you would not defend if others started on them. Today, say one accurate good thing about that person, out loud, to someone else. You do not need to change your opinion. You only need to notice that the opinion was never tested.

studies.title: Four Names And A Warning
studies.meaning: The dispute in the Fire is confirmed as real, and then the address turns outward with two instructions to speak. What the messenger is told to say about himself is minimal: a warner, nothing more. What he is told to say about God is four names in two pairs, and the pairing is the point. The One who overcomes is also the Lord of everything between the heavens and the earth, and the Mighty is the Much Forgiving. Then the message is called great news, and the listeners are told they are turning from it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the surah has been answering a specific objection since its opening: that one man from among them should claim to speak for God, and that the many gods should be reduced to one. These ayat give the reply in its shortest form. No occasion is reported for them individually. The closing instruction, that the message is great news being turned away from, addresses an audience that had heard it and chosen not to engage.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from a verb meaning to overcome completely. Placed immediately after the name for oneness, it answers the question the objectors kept asking, which was not whether God exists but whether one God is enough.

Another intensive form, from a root meaning to cover over. It is set directly against the name for overwhelming might in the same line, so the surah refuses to let power and pardon be described as opposites.
Not ordinary information. This noun is used of accounts that change the hearer's situation, and the same phrase heads a short surah about what people were questioning each other over.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News travelled by mouth in Arabia, and the word for an important report meant something that arrived and changed what you did next: a raid coming, a caravan lost, a treaty broken, a death in the family. A man who carried such news to a settlement was heard immediately, whatever his rank. What these ayat describe is that kind of announcement being made in a market where everyone simply walked on.
studies.didYouKnow: The name for irresistible power occurs six times in the Quran and is never used alone. In every one of those places it follows immediately after the name for oneness, so the Book always states that God is one and that God overcomes in the same breath. The phrase for a great report appears here and at the head of a much later short surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes prophecy small and God large in the same breath, which is its argument. The messenger is stripped of every claim except delivery, so nothing in the message depends on his standing. Then the names do the work. Two of them describe unopposable power and two describe lordship and pardon, and holding all four together is what monotheism costs: the frightening God and the forgiving God cannot be kept in separate places.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same two names to close an argument about whether God could take a son.
Opens on the same phrase for a great report, there as the thing people keep disputing.
States the messengers' role in the same minimal terms, as bringers of good news and warning.

studies.applyIt: Pick the name in this passage that is hardest for you to hold, the overwhelming one or the forgiving one, and spend a minute deciding why. Most people lean on one and quietly drop the other. Then, when you next say a short prayer today, say both. Not as a formula. As a correction to whichever half you have been leaving out.

studies.title: No Knowledge Of The Highest Assembly
studies.meaning: The Adam narrative is introduced as evidence rather than as a story. The messenger first states what he does not have: any access of his own to the dispute among the highest assembly. All he has is what is sent to him, and what is sent makes him a plain warner. Only then does the account begin, with the announcement to the angels and the two conditions attached to it, forming and then breathing. The argument is in the order: a man who could not know this is telling it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The objection running through this surah is that the speaker is a man from among them with no credentials, and these ayat answer it with the one credential he claims. The commentators differ over what the dispute among the highest assembly refers to, some reading it as the exchange about the creation of Adam that follows, others as a separate matter. They record both without deciding.

keyTerms.note: A word for a council of notables, the men whose opinion decided a matter, qualified by the adjective for highest. The Quran uses the same term for the chiefs of Pharaoh and of Mecca, so the image is a governing circle.

A verb for making something even, level and rightly balanced. It describes completion of shape rather than the first act of making, and the command to bow is attached to what comes after it, not to the clay.

Earth mixed with water, the cheapest building material in Arabia and the one used for ordinary walls. The word is chosen for its plainness, and the refusal that follows will turn that plainness into an argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every Arabian settlement had its assembly, a place where the heads of families sat and decisions were taken by men whose names everyone knew. Mecca had one beside the sanctuary. To say that one has no knowledge of a council is a very particular claim in that world: it means the speaker was not in the room, and nobody who was in the room told him. The listeners understood exactly what was being denied.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the highest assembly occurs twice in the Quran, here and in one other Meccan surah, where it describes something the rebellious cannot listen in on. Both places attach it to eavesdropping or access. The term itself is an everyday political word in Arabic for the council of a town, lifted upward by a single adjective.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is defended here on the narrowest possible ground. No miracle is offered, no character reference, no appeal to the messenger's honesty. The claim is simply that certain information has no human route, so its presence in his mouth is itself the evidence. That also fixes the limits of prophecy: what he knows, he knows because it was given, and the passage says so before it says anything else.

crossReferences.why: Gives the only other mention of the highest assembly, describing it as guarded against listeners.
Makes the same argument after the Joseph account, that the teller was not present when it happened.
Repeats the same two conditions, the shaping and the breathing, before the command to bow.

studies.applyIt: Notice, once today, the difference between something you know and something you were told. Take one fact you are confident about, a bit of news or a claim about a person, and trace it back to where it entered your head. This passage opens by drawing exactly that line. Most of what anyone carries is received, and knowing which is which is a small discipline.

studies.title: What I Made With My Hands
studies.meaning: Compliance is stated twice over. The angels bowed, all of them, together, with two separate words for totality, so the exception that follows is isolated as completely as language allows. Then the question put to the refuser is unusual. It offers him two possibilities rather than one: was this arrogance, or was he genuinely of a higher rank. The second option is real, and it is the one he will not claim. The commentators note that he answers neither question directly.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the surah closes with this account after a long sequence of prophets who were tested and held. No occasion is reported. The placement is deliberate: a chapter that has been arguing with men who considered themselves too important to follow one of their own ends by narrating the first refusal made on exactly those grounds. The classical commentators read the two as a single argument.

keyTerms.note: A word for entirety added after another word that already says all. Arabic uses the doubling to close off any reading in which some were absent, which is why the single exception in the next line stands out so sharply.

A dual form, and the only place in the Quran where the making of the human being is described this way. The commentators are agreed that no bodily limbs are meant and read it as an expression of direct attention and honour.

A participle for those who are genuinely elevated, occurring once in the Quran, here. Offering it as an alternative to arrogance concedes that a real rank would have been a real answer, which is what makes the question sharp.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rank in Arabia was inherited and physical. A man's place at a gathering, the order in which he was served, who greeted whom first: all of it was settled before anyone spoke, and a claim to precedence was tested against ancestry that could be recited aloud. The question in this passage borrows that whole system and puts it to a being who has no genealogy. He is asked, in effect, to produce his line, and he changes the subject to material.
studies.didYouKnow: Two expressions in this short passage occur nowhere else in the Quran. The phrase about creating with two hands is used here alone, of Adam, and the participle for those who are genuinely exalted appears in this ayah and in no other. The Book tells the story of the first refusal seven times, and only this telling carries either phrase.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The honour given to the human being is located in the act of making, not in the material or in any achievement. That is why the question is about rank and not about obedience. It also sets a pattern the Quran keeps: dignity is conferred from above and cannot be earned or forfeited by comparison with someone else. And the offer of a second possible answer shows that the objection is being taken seriously enough to be refuted rather than simply overruled.

crossReferences.why: States the honouring of the children of Adam directly, without narrative, as a conferred preference.
Tells the same moment with the same two conditions, and records the refusal as a refusal of company.
Gives the shortest version, three verbs, and names the category the refusal placed him in.

studies.applyIt: The next time you catch yourself ranking someone below you, notice which measure you used. Money, accent, education, job, family. Then ask whether you would accept that same measure if it were turned around. You do not have to resolve anything. The passage simply shows that the first refusal in creation was a comparison, and comparisons feel like facts from the inside.

studies.title: The Comparison That Ended Him
studies.meaning: Five ayat, five speeches, and the exchange is over almost before it starts. The refusal is finally explained, and the explanation is a comparison of raw materials presented as self evident. The reply does not argue with it. Expulsion and a curse to the Day of Judgement are stated, and then something unexpected happens: the one expelled asks for something, and is answered. What he asks for is worth weighing. He has direct access and uses it to request time, not pardon.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just presented a series of prophets who were given hardship and turned back to God with it, and this account is set immediately after them as the opposite case. No occasion is reported. The commentators treat the sequence as the surah's closing argument to the chiefs of the city, whose objection had been about rank from the first ayat onward.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to stone or pelt, used of driving away a stray animal or an unwelcome person. The word names an expulsion carried out with force rather than a sentence pronounced from a distance.

The refusal is delivered, and the very next word of address is still a claim of lordship. The commentators note that nothing in this account denies God; what is disputed throughout is an instruction, never the one giving it.
A passive participle from a verb meaning to look toward and so to wait. The grant is put passively, which places him among a group rather than granting him anything personal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion was the heaviest penalty an Arabian community had short of killing. A man cast out of his tribe lost protection, water rights and the standing that let him trade, and the formula for it was public and final. Poets recorded such cases for generations. The vocabulary in these ayat is that vocabulary: driven off, cursed, put outside. What the first audience heard was not a metaphysical scene but a legal one they had watched happen.
studies.didYouKnow: The request and its answer are recorded in three surahs. The request is worded identically in all three, but in two of them the answer adds a phrase the request never used: until the day of the known appointed time. The classical commentators discuss the difference between the day people are raised and that appointed day at length, and do not close it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two things that are usually assumed to travel together. Belief that God exists, is Lord, created him and can grant requests is all present here and none of it helps. What is missing is submission, and the account treats that as the whole difference. It also shows a request from an avowed enemy being answered, which says something uncomfortable and important: being given what one asks for is not a sign of approval.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same exchange with the same comparison, and grants the delay in a shorter form.
Names the refusal and its cause without reporting any conversation at all.
Shows the same figure abandoning the person he persuaded, saying he fears God.

studies.applyIt: Think of an instruction you resisted recently at work or at home, and separate two questions you probably ran together. Was the instruction wrong, or did you dislike who gave it. Write one sentence for each. The passage turns on that separation, and most people find that when they pull the two apart honestly, only one of them had any content.

studies.title: And The Truth I Speak
studies.meaning: The vow is sworn by an attribute of the one being defied, which is the strangest feature of the passage. Then it exempts a group described not as people who purified themselves but as people who were made pure, so the exception is conceded to God before anyone contests it. The reply answers an oath with a declaration about truth, repeating the word twice in two different grammatical positions, and the classical readers record more than one way of voicing the first. The threat that follows is conditional on following.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah that began with men of the city urging each other to stand firm by their gods. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators read the whole account as placed here for the listener rather than for its own sake: a threat is quoted, its limit is stated in the same breath, and the surah then turns straight back to the messenger and his wage.

keyTerms.note: An oath sworn on a divine attribute, the ordinary Arabic form for a binding vow. Swearing by the power of the one being disobeyed concedes that power in the act of defying it, which the commentators note as the flaw in the boast.

A passive participle from a root meaning to make something unmixed. The passive matters: it names people who were purified rather than people who achieved purity, so the exception rests on God rather than on their resistance.

The word appears twice in one short line, carrying two different case endings and so two different jobs in the sentence. The classical readers transmit more than one voicing of the first, and the tafsir works discuss each at length.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath in seventh century Arabia was a public instrument, not a private feeling. Men swore by the lord of a shrine, by their fathers, by the sanctuary, and a broken oath was a matter for arbitration and compensation. The object a man swore by declared what he actually held sacred, which is why the Quran pays close attention to what an oath names. The vow quoted in these ayat gives its own answer to that question.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for truth is written twice in the same four word ayah, and in the standard text the two carry different vowel endings, which is unusual even in a Book full of close grammatical detail. Readers in the classical tradition transmit more than one voicing for the first of them, and the commentaries spend more space on this line than on the threat that follows it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A total claim is made and then bounded from two directions in four lines. The one making it names an exception himself, and the reply names the condition on which anyone falls inside the threat: following. Between them, nothing is left that operates without consent. That is the Quran's consistent position on this subject, and it is why the figure is described elsewhere as having no authority at all, only an invitation.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same admission in his own mouth at the end, that he only called and they answered.
Gives the identical claim and exception, and states plainly that there is no authority over God's servants.
Locates the reach of that influence precisely, in those who take him as an ally.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the oaths in your own speech today. I swear, honestly, I promise you. Count them for one conversation. Most of them arrive where a plain sentence would have done, and the habit quietly says that your ordinary words need propping up. Try dropping them for an afternoon and letting the statement stand on its own.

studies.title: I Ask You No Wage
studies.meaning: Three short ayat close the surah, and each removes a suspicion rather than adding a claim. First money: nothing is being charged. Then manner: the word used denies affectation, the pose of a man producing more than he has. Then scope: this is a reminder for all the worlds, which widens the address beyond the city arguing with him. The last line is a deferral, telling the listeners they will learn what the message was after a time, without saying how long.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the three suspicions answered here were live ones. Poets and soothsayers in Arabia worked for payment, and a man delivering oracular speech was expected to take a fee. The surah has already recorded the chiefs walking away and telling each other this was something invented. These closing ayat answer the accusation without repeating it, and then place the whole message beyond the quarrel that produced it.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary commercial word for payment for work done. The same denial is put in the mouth of one prophet after another across the Quran, always in the same commercial vocabulary, never in the language of piety.
A participle for someone forcing an effort, taking on what is not his and making a show of it. It occurs once in the Quran, here, and it denies a pose rather than a lie.
A deliberately vague noun for a stretch of time of no stated length. The commentators read it as death, or the victory that came later, or the resurrection, and they list the readings without ruling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's economy ran on fees and shares. Guides took a cut, poets were rewarded by the tribes they praised, custodians of the sanctuary drew income from pilgrims, and every service had a known price. A man who spoke publicly and took nothing was outside the system and therefore hard to place. That is part of why the question of payment comes up so often in the Quran's accounts of prophets and their audiences.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical commentaries preserve a report in which an early Muslim, asked about a rare Quranic word he did not know, answered by quoting this ayah, using it to mean that admitting ignorance is better than manufacturing an answer. The word itself occurs once in the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is defined at the end of this surah entirely by what it is not. Not paid, not performed, not local. Removing the fee removes the motive an audience most readily supplies, and removing the pose removes the other one, that the speaker is enjoying the role. What remains is a message and a deadline, and the deadline is left unspecified, so the listener is given no way to wait comfortably for it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same denial of payment in Noah's mouth, in a surah that repeats it for five prophets.
Instructs the Prophet to say the same thing about the guidance given to earlier messengers.
Closes another surah with the same claim, that this is only a reminder to the worlds.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing today that you would normally mention. A favour you did, an hour you stayed late, a bill you quietly paid. Do not mention it. Not to be humble, and not so that someone notices you did not mention it. Just let it stand undeclared for a day and see what that feels like.
